title: Introduction to Linguistics
summary: Discover how language works: phonetics and phonology including clicks and tone, morphology with Swahili examples, syntax and word order, semantics and pragmatics, sociolinguistics, African language families and acquisition.
audience: Language students, teachers, translators and anyone fascinated by language

body.p: Linguistics is the scientific study of language: how sounds, words and sentences are structured, how meaning works, how languages are learned, how they vary in society and how they change over time. Linguists describe how people actually use language, rather than prescribing "correct" forms.

list: Phonetics and phonology: speech sounds and sound systems.
Morphology: the structure of words.
Syntax: the structure of sentences.
Semantics and pragmatics: meaning, literal and in context.
Sociolinguistics: language in society.
Psycholinguistics and acquisition: language in the mind and how children learn it.
Historical linguistics: how languages change and are related.

body.p: Africa is one of the most linguistically diverse regions on Earth, with around two thousand languages, making it a rich place to study language. Every language, including those without long written traditions, has complex, rule-governed grammar.

body.tip: Listen to how people around you speak in different settings; you are already observing linguistic variation.

body.p: Phonetics describes how speech sounds are produced and heard. The International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) gives one symbol for each sound, so any language can be written precisely; for example [ʃ] is the "sh" sound in "shop".

list: Consonants are described by place (lips, teeth, palate…), manner (stop, fricative, nasal…) and voicing (vocal cords vibrating or not): [p] and [b] differ only in voicing.
Vowels are described by tongue height, frontness and lip rounding.
Click consonants, rare worldwide, are part of the sound systems of isiXhosa and isiZulu (written c, q and x) and of Khoe and San languages.
Tone: in tone languages pitch distinguishes words. Yoruba has three level tones, so the same syllables with different tones can mean entirely different things.

body.p: Phonology studies which sound differences matter in a language. A minimal pair is two words differing in only one sound, such as English "pin" and "bin", showing that /p/ and /b/ are separate phonemes in English. Sound patterns differ: a difference meaningful in one language may be ignored in another.

body.tip: Say "pin" and "bin" with your hand on your throat; you will feel the vibration for the voiced [b].

body.p: A morpheme is the smallest unit of meaning. Words may contain one or several.

list: "Unhappiness" has three morphemes: un- (not) + happy + -ness (state).
Free morphemes stand alone (happy); bound morphemes must attach (un-, -ness).
Inflection changes grammatical form (walk, walked); derivation creates new words (teach, teacher).

body.p: Many Bantu languages build long words from many morphemes. In Swahili, "ninakupenda" (I love you) is ni- (I) + -na- (present tense) + -ku- (you) + -penda (love): four morphemes in one word. Nouns belong to noun classes marked by prefixes: "mtoto" (child) and "watoto" (children) differ by the class prefix m- versus wa-, and the class affects agreement across the sentence.
Languages differ in how much they pack into words: some, like Mandarin, use mostly single-morpheme words; others, like Swahili or Turkish, join many morphemes together.

body.tip: Break unfamiliar words into parts; morphology makes vocabulary learning much faster.

body.p: Syntax studies how words combine into phrases and sentences. Sentences have hierarchical structure, not just word order: in "the old man's dog", "old" describes the man, not the dog, because of how the phrase is built.

list: English, Swahili and Yoruba are mainly subject-verb-object (SVO): "Amina reads books".
Japanese, Hindi and Amharic are mainly subject-object-verb (SOV).
Some languages, such as classical Arabic and Welsh, often put the verb first (VSO).
Agreement, case marking and particles also show who did what to whom.

body.p: "I saw the man with the telescope" has two structures: either I used the telescope, or the man had it. Syntax explains such ambiguity and how listeners resolve it using context.
All humans acquire syntax naturally, and children create new sentences they have never heard, showing that language involves rules, not just memorised phrases.

body.tip: Compare word order in two languages you know; it reveals syntactic differences instantly.

body.p: Semantics studies literal meaning: word meanings and how they combine. Pragmatics studies meaning in context: what speakers intend and how listeners interpret it.

list: Synonyms: similar meanings (big, large).
Antonyms: opposites (hot, cold).
Hyponyms: types of a broader term (mango is a hyponym of fruit).
Polysemy: one word, related meanings (the head of a person, the head of a school).

body.p: "Can you pass the salt?" is literally a question about ability but is understood as a request. Context, shared knowledge and politeness shape meaning. Cultures differ in directness, greetings and how to show respect, for example through honorific forms or indirect requests. Misunderstandings between speakers of different backgrounds are often pragmatic rather than grammatical.

body.tip: When a message seems rude, consider whether it reflects different politeness norms rather than intent.

lessons.title: Language in society, families and acquisition

list: Dialects and accents vary by region and social group; none is linguistically superior.
Multilingualism is normal for most of the world's people; code-switching between languages mid-conversation is a skilled practice.
Language policy decides which languages are used in schools, courts and government, affecting access and opportunity.
Language endangerment: many languages are losing speakers; documentation and community use help preserve them.

body.p: Africa's languages are usually grouped into major families: Niger-Congo (including the Bantu languages, Yoruba and Igbo), Afroasiatic (including Arabic, Amharic and Hausa), Nilo-Saharan (including Dholuo and Kanuri), and the Khoe and San languages, which are now treated as several separate families. Related languages share vocabulary and grammar inherited from a common ancestor.

Children acquire their first languages naturally through interaction, passing through stages of babbling, single words and two-word combinations. Research supports mother-tongue-based early education, which helps children learn to read and later learn additional languages.

body.tip: Ask an older relative about words they used that young people no longer use; you are observing language change.
